title: Implicit and explicit coercion (+, ToNumber, ToString)
hook: JavaScript quietly converts values between types when you use `+`, comparisons, or `if`. Understanding ToNumber, ToString, and ToBoolean stops the `[] + []` surprises.

blocks.text: **Coercion** is the automatic or manual conversion of a value from one type to another. The ECMAScript specification defines abstract operations: **ToNumber** (e.g. `'42'` → `42`), **ToString** (e.g. `42` → `'42'`), and **ToBoolean** (e.g. `''` → `false`). The `+` operator is the famous fork: if either operand is a string, it does string concatenation; otherwise it converts both sides with ToNumber and adds. C# rejects most implicit cross-type math at compile time; JavaScript performs it at run time.

entries.plainDefinition: Automatic conversion the language performs for you — like `'5' - 2` becoming `3`.
Conversion you trigger on purpose with functions or operators.
Spec algorithm that converts any value to a number. `''` → `0`, `'hello'` → `NaN`, `true` → `1`.
Converts objects to primitives via `valueOf` then `toString`. Drives `[1,2] + 3` → `'1,23'`.

blocks.text: Form inputs return strings. `if (input + 1 > 10)` concatenates instead of adding when `input` is `'9'`. API query params arrive as strings — always parse with `Number()`, `parseInt()`, or `BigInt()` explicitly. Template literals and `String()` are safer than relying on `+` for building messages. In C#, `int.Parse` or `TryParse` makes the conversion visible; JavaScript hides it inside operators unless you are disciplined.

blocks.title: Safe conversion helpers
blocks.body: Numbers: `Number(x)`, `parseInt(x, 10)`, `parseFloat(x)`. Strings: `String(x)`, template literals `` `${x}` ``. Booleans: `Boolean(x)` or `!!x` when you intend truthiness. Avoid `new Number()` / `new String()` — they create objects.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Is either operand a string (or becomes one)?
items.body: If yes → ToString both sides and concatenate. `'5' + 2` → `'52'`.

items.title: Other operators usually use ToNumber
items.body: `-`, `*`, `/`, `%`, and relational comparisons coerce to number (with exceptions for `==` — see topic 4).

diagram.title: Coercion paths for + operator
diagram.source:
flowchart TD
  A["a + b"] --> B{"Either primitive string?"}
  B -->|yes| C["ToString both → concatenate"]
  B -->|no| D{"Either object?"}
  D -->|yes| E["ToPrimitive → retry"]
  D -->|no| F["ToNumber both → add"]
  E --> B

snippet.label: String vs number with +
snippet.code:
console.log('5' + 2);    // '52' — string wins
console.log('5' - 2);    // 3 — subtraction forces ToNumber
console.log(5 + '2');    // '52'
console.log(5 - '2');    // 3
console.log(true + 1);   // 2 — true → 1
console.log(null + 1);   // 1 — null → 0
console.log(undefined + 1); // NaN — undefined → NaN
snippet.explanation: Line 1: if either side is string, `+` concatenates. Line 2: `-` always uses ToNumber. Lines 6–8: boolean, null, and undefined have numeric mappings in ToNumber.

snippet.label: Object coercion via ToPrimitive
snippet.explanation: Lines 1–4: arrays/objects convert via `toString()` for `+` when no string operand. Lines 6–11: custom `valueOf`/`toString` change coercion — rare in production but interview-relevant.

snippet.label: Explicit conversion — production style
snippet.explanation: Lines 5–6: explicit `Number()` beats implicit coercion for form data. Line 9: `parseInt` needs radix `10` to avoid octal surprises on old strings. Lines 12–16: validate before math — C# `TryParse` equivalent pattern.

blocks.title: Coercion across languages
rows: `Number()` at run time; TS checks at compile time
Same as JS at run time

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Using `+` to add form field values that are strings. Forgetting radix in `parseInt('08', 10)`. Relying on `==` with mixed types (see topic 4). Using `new Number(5)` — creates an object where `typeof` is `'object'`, breaking strict checks.

blocks.text: Coercion is specified, not random — but the spec is long. `+` checks `IsString` before `ToPrimitive`. Abstract Relational Comparison (`<`, `>`) converts both sides to primitives, then to numbers if neither is string. `==` uses a different algorithm (see equality topic) that includes type coercion. `Object.is` and `===` skip coercion entirely. In production, lint rules (`eqeqeq`, `@typescript-eslint/strict-boolean-expressions`) ban implicit coercion in conditionals. The `valueOf`/`toString` order matters: for `+`, `ToPrimitive` tries `valueOf` first for non-dates; `String(obj)` tries `toString` first.

blocks.title: Tradeoffs at senior level
rows: Empty string is falsy AND numeric zero
null is falsy but coerces to 0 in math

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Saying coercion is 'random' without citing the spec path. Not knowing `+` prefers string concatenation. Claiming `parseInt('08')` is always 8 (old octal). Ignoring that `null` coerces to 0 in numeric context.

interviewTakeaways: `+` concatenates if either operand is a string; otherwise ToNumber and add.
ToNumber: '' → 0, null → 0, undefined → NaN, true → 1, false → 0.
Objects coerce via ToPrimitive (valueOf / toString) before + and comparisons.
Prefer explicit Number(), String(), Boolean() over relying on operators.
60s: + picks string concat or numeric add. ToNumber maps null to 0, undefined to NaN. Objects use ToPrimitive.
commonPitfalls: Weak: 'JavaScript coercion is unpredictable.' Strong: 'Spec-defined: + checks for string, else ToNumber; objects use ToPrimitive.'
Using + to sum form inputs that are strings — concatenation bug.
Strong answer: 'Explicit parse at boundaries. + is concat if any string. null→0 in math but falsy in if.'

jsTsCorrelations.note: TypeScript flags `'5' + 2` at compile time. At run time (or in .js files) coercion still happens — TS does not change runtime behavior.
C# requires explicit `int.Parse` or casts for string→number. No silent `'5' + 2` concat — compile-time safety.
